info.title: Hanzo Cloud API
info.description: Package network mounts the Hanzo Cloud NETWORKING surface: the tenant's Hanzo Zero Trust footprint — the overlay network, its routers and its services — served as clean, org-scoped REST off the unified cloud binary and fronting the Hanzo Zero Trust controller (hanzoai/zt, an ZT-based fabric).

get.summary: Lists the invites, newest first: each one's id, status, note, issue time, expiry and who issued it.
get.description:
Lists the invites, newest first: each one's id, status, note, issue
time, expiry and who issued it. It never returns a code, nor anything a code can
be got from. It is a SuperAdmin's; another caller is refused 403, audited. A
status is active, revoked, or expired for an active invite past its expiry.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description:
Limit is how many invites a page holds; 0 means 200 and nothing above 1000 is
honoured.

parameters.name: cursor
parameters.description:
Cursor is the previous page's next; empty for the first page. It is opaque: a
value that was not given as a next is a 400.

post.summary: Issues invite codes and answers them in clear, once.
post.description:
Issues invite codes and answers them in clear, once. It is a
SuperAdmin's, and no one else may call it: another caller is refused 403 and the
refusal is audited. Each code is HNZ- and ten characters of Crockford base32, shown
as HNZ-XXXXX-XXXXX, from crypto/rand and unique among the codes issued; only an HMAC
of it is stored, so a code
shown here and lost is revoked by id and issued again. The audit trail takes the
intent, with the count and the note and never a code, before anything is written,
and answers 503 with nothing written when it cannot.

A count is 1 to 100 and a life 1 to 365 days, and an absent one is one code for
30 days; anything else is 400.

delete.summary: Revokes one invite and answers 204: its code stops verifying at once.
delete.description:
Revokes one invite and answers 204: its code stops verifying at once.
Revoking one that is already revoked is the same 204, and an id that names no
invite is 404. It is a SuperAdmin's; another caller is refused 403, audited. Every
attempt is on the audit trail with its outcome, and the trail takes the intent before
an invite is changed and answers 503 with nothing changed when it cannot.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: ID is the invite id from the path, as issue and the list show it.

get.summary: Returns the caller's org overlay network on the Zero Trust fabric.
get.description:
Returns the caller's org overlay network on the Zero Trust fabric.

The org has at most ONE overlay, projected from the edge-routers tagged with its
"org-<org>" role attribute: nodes is the real router count and status is
"connected" once at least one router has dialed home, "provisioning" while none
has. An org with no routers gets an empty list, never a fabricated network.

The read degrades rather than erroring: a deployment with no ZT credential, and a
controller that cannot be reached, both answer 200 with an empty list so the
console's Networks page renders a clean empty state instead of an error.

get.summary: Returns the fabric identities the caller's org owns.
get.description:
Returns the fabric identities the caller's org owns.

One row per identity tagged with the org's "org-<org>" role attribute, each
naming the IAM subject it logs in as. A steward sees every one; a plain member
sees only its own, since who else is on the org's network is not a member's
to read, and a plain member's API key, which holds no identity, is refused.

A tenancy read over the full inventory, so like the mesh list it does NOT
degrade: an unconfigured deployment answers 503.

post.summary: Puts the caller on the org's overlay as its own IAM subject.
post.description:
Puts the caller on the org's overlay as its own IAM subject.

The identity is the one whose externalId is the caller's `sub`, admitted by
the controller's "iam" auth policy: the caller logs in to the fabric with its
own IAM access token, and nothing is enrolled. It is named by the subject
unless a name is given, and carries the org's "org-<org>" role attribute plus
any supplied roles — each scoped to the org, and a "<service>-host" role
refused unless the org has published that service. Roles are a steward's to
take: a plain member joins with the org role alone, and asking for more is
403 before the controller is written.

An API key is refused 403: the fabric admits an IAM access token, a person's
or an application's, and a key has none to log in with.

IDEMPOTENT: a caller who already has an identity gets the same one back, with
any of these roles it lacked added — which is how one person's identity comes
to serve every org they act in.

A write, so it does not degrade: an unconfigured deployment answers 503.

delete.summary: Takes one of the org's fabric identities out of the org.
delete.description:
Takes one of the org's fabric identities out of the org.

The identity's "org-<org>" role and every role scoped to the org are
removed and the rest is left alone, so an identity another org shares keeps
working there. The identity itself is deleted when no org role is left on
it, or when the caller IS its IAM subject — a person may always remove
themselves.

An id belonging to another org — or to nothing — is 404 before any write
reaches the controller: whether an identity exists is itself a cross-tenant
fact, and a delete may only ever act on what the caller could list, which for
a plain member is its own identity. A fabric administrator is the
controller's own and is refused.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description:
ID is the identity id from the path. The URL is the addressing authority,
so it binds from there whatever else the request carries.

post.summary: Says whether an invite code is live: {"valid": true} or {"valid": false}, and nothing else.
post.description:
Says whether an invite code is live: {"valid": true} or {"valid":
false}, and nothing else. It never says why a code is not valid: a code that was
never issued, one that is not shaped like a code, one that was revoked and one that
has expired get the same status and the same body, and it says nothing of who issued
a code. Verifying does not consume the code and does not spend it, and it needs no
account. Nothing on the server enforces an invite until redemption exists; the
operations that will need one will answer with the problem type invite_required.

A deployment that cannot hold invites, or has issued none yet, answers 503; then a
caller past ten requests an hour is 429, a body over 4 KiB 413 and a missing code or a
body that is not JSON 400, in that order. A caller that has missed five times in an
hour is refused 429 until the window passes, whatever it asks, so the refusal says
nothing about whether a code would have been valid, and Retry-After says when to come
back. The limits are per network address (an IPv6 /64, with the /48 around it counted
at sixteen times as much): clients behind one address share them, and so do callers
whose address is unknown.

get.summary: Returns the Zero Trust routers the caller's org owns.
get.description:
Returns the Zero Trust routers the caller's org owns.

One row per real ZT edge-router tagged with the org's "org-<org>" role attribute,
carrying the controller's own health signal: "online" when connected, "disabled"
when administratively disabled, "offline" otherwise. region is filled only from a
"region-<slug>" role attribute and omitted when the router carries none, so the
column renders "—" rather than a guess.

The read degrades rather than erroring: a deployment with no ZT credential, and a
controller that cannot be reached, both answer 200 with an empty list.

get.summary: Returns the Zero Trust edge services the caller's org owns.
get.description:
Returns the Zero Trust edge services the caller's org owns.

One row per real ZT edge service tagged with the org's "org-<org>" role
attribute: mtls is "required" when the service mandates end-to-end encryption and
"enabled" otherwise (the fabric always mutually authenticates every link), and
status is "active" because a listed service is a configured, dialable entry. A
service tagged for another org, or tagged for none, is invisible here.

Unlike the network and router reads this does NOT degrade: an unconfigured
deployment answers 503 and an unreachable controller surfaces the upstream's
status, so a mesh page never renders "no services" for a fabric it simply could
not read.

post.summary: Puts a name on the org's overlay: a fabric service forwarding to host:port on whichever of the org's devices carries the "<name>-host" role, dialable at "<name>.<org>.zt" by any of the org's identities — and by the cloud's own, which is what lets a BYO cluster's apiserver be attached to the fleet with a ".zt" kubeconfig.
post.description:
Puts a name on the org's overlay: a fabric service forwarding
to host:port on whichever of the org's devices carries the "<name>-host"
role, dialable at "<name>.<org>.zt" by any of the org's identities — and by
the cloud's own, which is what lets a BYO cluster's apiserver be attached to
the fleet with a ".zt" kubeconfig.

Answers 201 with the service and its DNS name. The objects behind it are
created in dependency order and unwound on failure, so a half-published
service never lingers on the fabric. Publishing is a steward's act — an
admin of the org or its own machine client — and a plain member is 403.

A write, so it does not degrade: an unconfigured deployment answers 503.

delete.summary: Takes a name off the org's overlay: the two policies, the service and its two configs that publishing made, in that order, and the "<name>-host" role from each of the org's identities — that role exists only for the bind policy to select, and a role naming no service is one the identities endpoint refuses to write.
delete.description:
Takes a name off the org's overlay: the two policies, the
service and its two configs that publishing made, in that order, and the
"<name>-host" role from each of the org's identities — that role exists
only for the bind policy to select, and a role naming no service is one
the identities endpoint refuses to write.

Only objects carrying this service's own names are deleted, so a policy
that selects the service by attribute is left alone. An id belonging to
another org — or to nothing — is 404 before any write, as for an identity.
Like publishing it is a steward's act, and a plain member is 403 before the
controller is read.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description:
ID is the service id from the path. The URL is the addressing authority,
so it binds from there whatever else the request carries.

post.summary: Puts an address or an X handle on the Hanzo Network waitlist and answers 202 pending.
post.description:
Puts an address or an X handle on the Hanzo Network waitlist and answers
202 pending. Nothing is mailed. It gives the same answer for an identifier that is
new and one asked for before, however often, and with the same headers, so it says
nothing about who is on the list; a repeat changes nothing, and the first entry
stands. An X handle is never looked up anywhere and no wallet address is taken. No
account is needed, and the entry keeps nothing about the caller. It also keeps
no email or handle: only a keyed HMAC digest of the identifier, under the one
invite secret with a domain of its own, is filed.

A deployment that cannot hold the waitlist, or has issued no invite yet, answers 503;
then a caller past ten requests an hour is 429 (with Retry-After), a body over 4 KiB
413, and a body that is not JSON, one with neither or both of email and xHandle, an
invalid one or a role that is not miner, builder, researcher or staker 400, in that
order. The ten an hour are per network address: clients behind one address share them,
and so do callers whose address is unknown. Nothing here is gated by an invite yet; the operations that will be answer with
the problem type invite_required.

get.summary: Returns one overlay network by id, scoped to the caller's org.
get.description:
Returns one overlay network by id, scoped to the caller's org.

The org has exactly one overlay network and its id is derived from the org, so
any other id — another tenant's, or one that does not exist — is 404 rather than
a peek across the tenant boundary. An org whose network exists but has no
edge-routers is 404 too, for the same reason the list is empty: there is no
overlay until something is on it.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description:
ID is the network id from the path. The URL is the addressing authority, so
it binds from there whatever else the request carries.

code.description:
Code is the invite code as the person has it, such as HNZ-7K9Q2-MXZ4P. Required.
Letters may be upper or lower case, the hyphens and spaces may be left out or put
anywhere, and I and L are read as 1 and O as 0, so a code copied by eye is found.
Anything that is not a code is not an error: it is answered as a code that is not
valid.

count.description: Count is how many codes to issue, 1 to 100. Absent or 0 means one.

expires_days.description: ExpiresDays is how many days the codes last, 1 to 365. Absent or 0 means 30.

note.description:
Note says what the codes are for, such as "launch week". Optional; one line,
clipped at 200 characters, and kept with each code.

invites.description: Invites are the new codes, in clear, once.

data.description: Data is the page; an empty array when none has been issued.

next.description: Next continues Data: pass it back as cursor. Empty on the last page.

valid.description:
Valid is true when the code was issued by this deployment, is not revoked and
has not expired, and false for every other reason, none of which is said.

created_by.description: CreatedBy is the SuperAdmin who issued it, by their IAM user.

expires_at.description: ExpiresAt is when it stops being valid.

id.description: ID is the invite's id, which a revoke names.

issued_at.description: IssuedAt is when it was issued.

note.description: Note is what the invite was issued for.

status.description: Status is active, revoked, or expired: an active invite past its expiry.

code.description:
Code is the invite code in clear, such as HNZ-7K9Q2-MXZ4P. This is the only time it
is shown: nothing keeps it.

expires_at.description: ExpiresAt is when the code stops being valid.

id.description:
ID is the invite's id, which the list shows and a revoke names. It is not the
code and does not reveal it.

status.description:
Status is "pending": the entry is on the waitlist and will be told when there
is room. It is the same answer whatever the identifier's standing.

email.description:
Email is the address to put on the waitlist: at most 320 characters, one
address. Send this or xHandle, never both.

locale.description:
Locale is the person's language as a BCP 47 tag, such as en or pt-BR. Optional;
any other value is recorded as none.

role.description:
Role is how the person comes: miner, builder, researcher or staker, in any case.
Required.

source.description:
Source is where the form was, such as hanzo.network/join. Optional; one line,
clipped at 200 characters.

xHandle.description:
XHandle is the X handle to put on the waitlist: one to fifteen letters, digits
and underscores, with or without a leading @. It is kept without the @ and in the
case it was given, and is never looked up. Send this or email, never both.

name.description:
Name is the identity's name within the org — a DNS label, stored on the
fabric as "<name>.<org>". Absent, the identity is named by the caller's
IAM subject. It is set when the identity is first made; an identity that
already exists keeps its name.

roles.description:
Roles are extra role attributes for the identity, each scoped to the
caller's org on the way in ("k3s-host" is written as "k3s-host.<org>") so
no caller can claim an attribute another tenant's policy selects. A role
of the form "<service>-host" makes this identity a HOST of that published
service — the bind policy from POST /v1/network/services selects exactly
that attribute — and is refused when the org has no such service. Only a
steward (an admin of the org or its own machine client) takes roles; a
plain member asking for one is 403.

identities.description: Identities is one row per fabric identity tagged with the caller's org role.

externalId.description:
ExternalID is the IAM subject the identity logs in as: the controller
admits a bearer whose `sub` equals it.

id.description: ID is the identity's fabric id — the key DELETE addresses.

name.description: Name is the identity's name within the org.

roles.description:
Roles are the identity's role attributes as the fabric holds them: the
"org-<org>" of every org it was ensured in, plus any org-scoped roles.

services.description: Services is one row per ZT edge service tagged with the caller's org role.

id.description: ID is the ZT edge service's id.

mtls.description:
Mtls is "required" when the service mandates end-to-end encryption, else
"enabled" — the fabric mutually authenticates every link, so it is never
truly off.

service.description: Service is the edge service's name.

status.description: Status is "active": a listed service is a configured, dialable mesh entry.

networks.description:
Networks holds the org's overlay network, or is empty when the org has no
edge-routers on the fabric (no nodes → no network, never a fabricated one).

id.description:
ID is the org-derived id of the overlay network — the key
GET /v1/network/{id} addresses.

name.description: Name is the org the overlay belongs to.

nodes.description: Nodes is how many edge-routers the org has on the fabric.

status.description:
Status is "connected" once at least one of the org's edge-routers is
online, else "provisioning" (routers exist but none has dialed home).

dns.description:
DNS is the name the fabric answers for this service — what a kubeconfig
server, or any client on the org's overlay, dials.

id.description: ID is the fabric service's id.

name.description: Name is the service's name within the org.

routers.description: Routers is one row per ZT edge-router tagged with the caller's org role.

id.description: ID is the ZT edge-router's id.

name.description: Name is the edge-router's name, falling back to its id when it has none.

region.description:
Region comes from a "region-<slug>" role attribute and is omitted when the
router carries none, so the column renders "—" rather than a guess.

status.description:
Status is the controller's own health signal: "online" when connected,
"disabled" when administratively disabled, "offline" otherwise.

host.description:
Host is where the HOSTING identity forwards a connection — an address the
host device itself can reach, "127.0.0.1" for a server on the device.

name.description:
Name is the service's name within the org — a DNS label. The fabric knows
the service as "<name>.<org>" and answers for it at "<name>.<org>.zt".

port.description: Port is the port beside Host, and the one the DNS name intercepts.

code.description: A stable token a client can branch on, when the refusal names one.

detail.description: What was refused, for a person to read.

bearer.description: The caller's credential, sent as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. It is either an access token minted by Hanzo IAM or an API key (pk-/sk-). X-Authorization, and HTTP Basic carrying the token as the password, are accepted spellings of the same header for clients that cannot set Authorization; a browser presents the session cookie instead. Every operation requires it unless it says `security: []`.
